raw_text:
The objective is to investigate and explain the persistent completion-time differences observed in sites using the same nominal work process. To achieve this, we'll examine measurable factors responsible for these differences and differentiate between competing explanations through observations.

Assumptions
1. Work processes are nominally standardized across the studied sites.
2. Completion times are relevant to productivity and efficiency in the context of this study.

Research design
We’ll employ a mixed-methods research design. Quantitative methods (e.g., statistical analyses, time-motion studies) will identify measurable factors contributing to completion-time variations, while qualitative methods (e.g., interviews, observation) will provide insights into nuances and idiosyncrasies of process implementation.

Data or evidence needed
1. Completion time records for each site over a consistent period.
2. Details of the purported same nominal work process at each site (standard operating procedures, tools, training received, etc.).
3. Observational data on working conditions, environmental factors, and employee behavior.
4. Qualitative data from interviews or focus groups with key personnel at each site.

Measurement
The completion times will be measured using directly observed timestamps or documented records to ensure accuracy. Workplace conditions, environmental factors, and employee behaviors will be operationally defined and behaviorally measured through surveys, interviews, and direct observation.

Analysis
Quantitative data will be analyzed with regression models and ANOVA tests to identify significant factors associated with completion time variation. Qualitative data will be thematically analyzed for patterns and insights.

Decision / stopping rule
We will continue data collection until saturation is achieved in qualitative findings, ensuring comprehensiveness. A predetermined sample size and statistical significance level (e.g., p < 0.05) will define when to conclude quantitative analyses.

Limitations
Given the mixed-methods approach, interpretation challenges may arise from correlating quantitative and qualitative findings. Furthermore, self-reported data in surveys and interviews could introduce biases. External factors, beyond our control, may also influence site performance, necessitating cautious generalizations from our findings.
